title: The blessing before study
hookLine: before learning, a blessing to be busy with words of Torah
tomorrow: Camp 3 close: your week has a shape

cards: Before a meal, many Jews say a blessing: bread gets one, fruit gets one, even water gets one. You've met those. But there's a blessing for something you can't eat.
Before opening a book of Torah, before the day's first lesson, traditional Jews stop and bless God, the way they would over bread. As if words were food.
And the Talmud tells a startling story about what happens when this blessing is skipped.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE YOU, LORD OUR GOD.
teach.b: The blessing opens like the ones over bread and fruit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam. Blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe.
Then: asher kid'shanu b'mitzvotav, who made us holy with his commandments, v'tzivanu la'asok b'divrei Torah, and commanded us to be busy with the words of Torah. That verb is the surprise. La'asok.
Not to read. Not to know. To be busy with, engaged in, occupied by.
The blessing doesn't ask you to finish Torah, or master it. It asks you to be in the middle of it, working on it, the way someone runs a shop.
Many prayer books follow it with a line asking that the words be sweet in our mouths, and in the mouths of our children.
In traditional practice, these blessings are said once in the morning, and they cover the whole day's learning. Now the startling story. The Talmud asks why the land was lost in ancient times.

teach.h: THEY DID NOT BLESS THE TORAH FIRST.
teach.b: It quotes the prophet Jeremiah asking the same thing, and answers in the name of the teacher Rav: because they did not bless the Torah first. They studied. They knew it.
But they didn't stop first and treat it as a gift.
One medieval commentator, the Ran, reads it this way: they studied, but didn't hold the Torah dear enough to bless it first. In that reading, the blessing is a doorway.
It marks the words as a gift before the study, and the argument, begins.

how: Traditional Jews say the blessings over Torah study each morning as part of the morning prayers, and many say them again before a class or a study session.

o: to master the whole Torah, start to end
to be busy with, or engaged in, Torah
to read Torah aloud before the whole room

games.q: the people in Jeremiah's day studied Torah and knew it well. according to the Talmud, what went wrong?
o: they did not bless the Torah first.
games.why: they learned it, but didn't stop to treat it as a gift. the blessing marks the words as a gift.

practice: Pick up anything you'll read today, a book, a letter, even a long message, or just picture it, and stop before the first word.

If you pray, you can say the blessing's opening words, Baruch atah Adonai, or the whole line; if you don't, take one breath and remember that words are a gift someone gave you. Then read one sentence slowly.

wordCard.voice: La'asok. To be busy with: the surprising verb in the blessing said before study, which asks only that you be busy with Torah's words.
